Sunlight warms the surface. Earth emits infrared; some energy escapes to space.ENERGY PATHS · NOT A SEALED LIDSunlightEARTH’S SURFACE · emits infrared energyInfraredRe-emittedTo spaceSomeenergyescapesNatural effectKey wordsclimate — patterns of weather over many yearsgreenhouse gas — gas that absorbs and emits infrared radiationmitigation — limiting warming by addressing its causesadaptation — adjusting to reduce harm from impactsbaseline — measurement before a changeRememberThe natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warmer than it would otherwise be.Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide.Extra greenhouse gases initially reduce energy loss to space, leading to warming.A local action check is not a measurement of global temperature change.Success looks likeLink a human activity to greenhouse gases and warming.Distinguish weather, climate, mitigation and adaptation.Use comparable before/after evidence without overstating what it proves.Activity → extra greenhouse gases → changed energy balance → warming → an effect. Use one response mode, not every available format.StageTimeFocusOpening2 minFollow the Warming Chain · ClassicArrival5 minFour clues to startStarter4 minDoes one day settle the question?I do7 minWatch, predict, explainWe do10 minMatch a scenario to a useful science actionYou do10 minUse the evidence yourselfExit2 minTwo small checksPreparation and accessUse diagrams, clean cards and fictional examples. No family carbon data, spending or pledges are required. Only adults authorise changes to school equipment. Never switch off safety lighting, necessary heating, ventilation, fridges or medical equipment.Scientific careGreenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared in different directions; energy still escapes to space. Extra greenhouse gases initially reduce outgoing energy at a given temperature; warming moves towards a new balance. This is not a sealed lid. One cold day neither proves nor disproves a long-term global trend. Land ice, not a floating ice cube analogy, is used for sea-level effects.Responsive teachingStart with what the pupil shows today. Use a fresh diagram or clue rather than asking for old work. The optional help request sits inside the We do or evidence review. Hear it, explain the possible adjustment, try it and check its effect. Choose the question before choosing a science word. Not every correct fact is relevant.MATCH THE QUESTION TO THE EVIDENCEWhich surface gave longertravel?Repeated distance tableWhy is a location indarkness?Fixed-light rotationmodelHow can extra CO₂ causewarming?Infrared energy modelKey wordsclaim — the answer you proposeevidence — observations or data used to support a claimreason — the science linking evidence to a claimrelevant — directly useful for this questionlimit — what the evidence cannot establishRememberA correct fact is not always relevant to a question.Use values and units, or a precise model observation.Separate what you observed from why you think it happened.An improved answer adds accurate science, not merely more words.Success looks likeSelect evidence that answers the actual question.Link a claim to an observation and a science reason.Keep a first response, then make one meaningful improvement.My answer is ___. In a controlled setup, resistance at contacts can affect how far the rover travels.Fixed light → Day/night question. LEFT marker faces light; RIGHT marker faces away.Rotating Earth → Day/night question. A place turns into and out of sunlight.Extra carbon dioxide → Warming question. More greenhouse gas can initially reduce net infrared energy loss.Long-term temperature → Warming question. Climate patterns are assessed over many years, not one cold morning.InvestigationSurface: smooth gives longer travel in these practice data (44–46 versus 18–20 cm); less resistance is a plausible explanation under controlled conditions, not a universal rule. Day/night: a location rotates towards/away from light. Climate: extra greenhouse gases alter net energy loss; one cold day is not a global trend.Review the claimEvidence must be relevant. Start from the evidence supplied here.Investigation plan4 min · Recheck the release and measurement method.20 min · Carry out or direct six safe trials, or analyse the supplied teaching dataset. Label your evidence source.2 min · Check controls, units and all raw values.6 min · Compare repeated distances, qualify the conclusion and improve one method detail.StepConsistent procedure1 · Set upOne secured ramp, rover and marked measurement origin2 · TrialRelease from the mark without pushing; allow it to stop3 · MeasureMeasure to the same rover point in cm; record the raw result4 · RepeatThree trials per surface; record any method issueSafe accessUse a low secured ramp on the floor or inside a bounded tray, one unpowered toy rover and a clear stop lane. W1 · Knowledge organiserLAUNCH · W9 · Lesson 1 · Shared resourceLearning objectiveDistinguish interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis, and explain why DNA is copied before division.Four-chromosome model: DNA copying in interphaseInterphase: DNA is copied4 unreplicated chromosomes4 replicated chromosomescopySymbols show DNA copies, not visible interphase chromosome shapes.Key wordsCell cycle — Growth, DNA copying and cell division.Interphase — The cell grows and copies its DNA before mitosis.Chromosome — A long DNA molecule packaged with proteins.Mitosis — Division of the nucleus into two genetically identical nuclei.Cytokinesis — Division of the cytoplasm to form two cells.Diploid — Two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent.Remember• DNA is copied before mitosis, during interphase.• Prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase describes mitosis.• Cytokinesis produces separate daughter cells.• Mitosis supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction.Success looks like• Order interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis.• Locate DNA copying before mitosis.• Explain how each daughter gets a complete set.W9_L1 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "arrival-supported": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEFour clues to startLAUNCH · W9 · Lesson 1 · SupportedName: ____________________Four checks. Point, speak, sign, draw, write or direct an adult. An adult may read or scribe your exact words. Choose one route; do not complete all three.1. LocateWhich part of a typical body cell contains chromosomes?Help: Read or point first. Use the cell diagram: membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus.2. PrepareWhat must happen to DNA before the cell divides?Help: Read or point first. Think about giving each new cell a full set.3. Cell numberOne cell divides once. How many daughter cells form?Help: Read or point first. Count the final outlines, not the chromosomes.4. ReasonWhy does a healing cut need new cells?Help: Read or point first. Connect replacement with repair.W9_L1 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "independent-supported": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEShow your understandingLAUNCH · W9 · Lesson 1 · SupportedName: ____________________Point, speak, sign, draw, write or direct an adult. An adult may read or scribe your exact words. Choose one route; do not complete all three.1. SequenceDraw or arrange the three main parts of the cycle.Help: Arrange these labels: cytokinesis / interphase / mitosis. Say: first ___, then ___, finally ___.2. W1 · Knowledge organiserLAUNCH · W9 · Lesson 2 · Shared resourceLearning objectiveSequence prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase using visible chromosome evidence.Four-chromosome model: DNA copying in interphaseInterphase: DNA is copied4 unreplicated chromosomes4 replicated chromosomescopySymbols show DNA copies, not visible interphase chromosome shapes.Key wordsCell cycle — Growth, DNA copying and cell division.Interphase — The cell grows and copies its DNA before mitosis.Chromosome — A long DNA molecule packaged with proteins.Mitosis — Division of the nucleus into two genetically identical nuclei.Cytokinesis — Division of the cytoplasm to form two cells.Diploid — Two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent.Remember• DNA is copied before mitosis, during interphase.• Prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase describes mitosis.• Cytokinesis produces separate daughter cells.• Mitosis supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction.Success looks like• Order prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.• Link each stage to chromosome evidence.• Distinguish an observation from an uncertain stage label.W9_L2 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "arrival-supported": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEFour clues to startLAUNCH · W9 · Lesson 2 · SupportedName: ____________________Four checks. W2 · Knowledge organiserLAUNCH · W10 · Lesson 1 · Shared resourceLearning objectiveExplain how division, elongation and differentiation contribute to growth in plants and animals.Cell division modelDivision increases cell number2 cells4 cellsKey wordsGrowth — An increase in size or mass.Division — One cell produces daughter cells.Elongation — A cell becomes longer.Differentiation — A cell develops specialised structures and functions.Stem cell — An unspecialised cell that can divide and differentiate.Meristem — A region containing dividing, unspecialised plant cells.Remember• Animals grow through cell division and differentiation.• Plants grow through division, elongation and differentiation.• Embryonic stem cells can form many cell types; most adult stem cells have more limited potential.• Meristems occur at growing root and shoot tips.Success looks like• Distinguish increased cell number from increased cell length.• Identify evidence of differentiation.• Explain plant growth using all three processes.W10_L1 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "arrival-supported": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEFour clues to startLAUNCH · W10 · Lesson 1 · SupportedName: ____________________Four checks. W2 · Knowledge organiserLAUNCH · W10 · Lesson 3 · Shared resourceLearning objectiveCalculate changes and interpret growth or stem-cell data without turning a pattern into a diagnosis or cure claim.Cell division modelDivision increases cell number2 cells4 cellsKey wordsGrowth — An increase in size or mass.Division — One cell produces daughter cells.Elongation — A cell becomes longer.Differentiation — A cell develops specialised structures and functions.Stem cell — An unspecialised cell that can divide and differentiate.Meristem — A region containing dividing, unspecialised plant cells.Remember• Animals grow through cell division and differentiation.• Plants grow through division, elongation and differentiation.• Embryonic stem cells can form many cell types; most adult stem cells have more limited potential.• Meristems occur at growing root and shoot tips.Success looks like• Calculate a change with the correct unit.• Read a fictional percentile chart without diagnosing.• Separate a marker result from a cure claim.W10_L3 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "arrival-supported": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEFour clues to startLAUNCH · W10 · Lesson 3 · SupportedName: ____________________Four checks. What is the increase?Help: Read or point first. After minus before.2. Percentage80 out of 100 cells show a marker. What percentage is this?Help: Read or point first. Out of 100 means percent.3. MeasureDoes a marker alone prove a cell is working normally?Help: Read or point first. A label and a function are different kinds of evidence.4. Growth chartWhat does the 50th percentile describe?Help: Read or point first. Informed consent, fairness and careful evidence matter. Adult stem cells avoid that particular embryo-source concern but usually have more limited potential. You may explain contrasting arguments without stating a personal belief.Three discussion cardsPossible benefitResearch could improve understanding or future treatments, but each benefit claim needs evidence.Embryo status and consentPeople differ about the moral status of early embryos. Informed, voluntary consent and clear oversight matter.Fairness and uncertaintyWho might benefit, who might bear risk, and what remains unknown?Discuss a reason, not a personYou can explain contrasting views, ask a private question or pass. W5 · Knowledge organiserLAUNCH · W13 · Lesson 2 · Shared resourceLearning objectiveConstruct a monohybrid Punnett square and explain how gametes combine to predict offspring genotypes.Two heterozygous parents Aa and AaTwo heterozygous parentsAaGenotype: AaAaGenotype: Aa×A and a are alleles of the same gene.Key wordsAllele — A version of a gene.Genotype — The allele combination for a gene.Phenotype — An observable characteristic.Dominant — Expressed in a heterozygote in this simple model.Recessive — Expressed when two recessive alleles are present in this model.Gamete — A sex cell with one allele for each gene in the model.Remember• Use the same letter for alleles of one gene: A and a.• AA and aa are homozygous; Aa is heterozygous.• A Punnett square predicts probabilities, not a fixed family pattern.• Most real human characteristics involve more than one gene and the environment.Success looks like• Put one allele in each gamete margin.• Combine one allele from each parent in every box.• Read a genotype probability from the completed square.W13_L2 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "arrival-supported": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEFour clues to startLAUNCH · W13 · Lesson 2 · SupportedName: ____________________Four checks. PairWhat does heterozygous Aa mean?Help: Read or point first. Compare the two alleles.2. GameteHow many alleles for this gene go in one gamete?Help: Read or point first. One parent contributes one to the offspring pair.3. OptionsWhich gamete alleles can an Aa parent produce?Help: Read or point first. Separate the pair, not copy Aa into every margin.4. CombineA gamete with A combines with a gamete with a. What is the offspring genotype?Help: Read or point first. State what remains uncertain.W14_L1 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "source-cards": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEApproved source cardsLAUNCH · W14 · Lesson 1 · Shared resourceThese are paraphrased classroom summaries, not quotations or individual medical advice. Check the full sources for further detail.Source A · NHS public informationCystic fibrosis is an inherited condition. Altered gene copies inherited from both parents affect the movement of salt and water in cells, causing thick, sticky mucus. This can affect the lungs and digestive system. Care is individualised. This summary does not predict any one person’s symptoms.Accessed 16 September 2026. Page review date is not asserted in this pack.https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cystic-fibrosis/Source B · NHS Genomics EducationCystic fibrosis usually results from pathogenic variants in both copies of CFTR. It follows autosomal recessive inheritance. When both parents are carriers, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of a child with the condition, a 50% chance of a carrier, and a 25% chance of neither altered copy in this model. Severity varies.Reviewed 12 March 2025; next review 12 March 2028. Accessed 16 September 2026.https://www.genomicseducation.hee.nhs.uk/genotes/knowledge-hub/cystic-fibrosis/The two sources have different audiences but are not wholly independent publishers.W14_L1 · Pupil resource · unmarked", "staff-1": "MADE BY MATT / LAUNCH SCIENCEStaff teaching cardLAUNCH · W14 · Lesson 1 · Shared resourceStageTimeTeacher focusArrival4 minFour clues to startStarter4 minChoose a first ideaI do5 minWatch the modelWe do5 minSort using the evidenceI do 24 minWork through one exampleWe do 24 minFind–Label–Map–GapIndependent10 minShow your understandingExit4 minTwo small checksPreparation and equal accessNo biological samples are needed. Check the full sources for further detail.Source A · NHS public informationCystic fibrosis is an inherited condition. Altered gene copies inherited from both parents affect the movement of salt and water in cells, causing thick, sticky mucus. This can affect the lungs and digestive system. Care is individualised. This summary does not predict any one person’s symptoms.Accessed 16 September 2026. Page review date is not asserted in this pack.https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cystic-fibrosis/Source B · NHS Genomics EducationCystic fibrosis usually results from pathogenic variants in both copies of CFTR. It follows autosomal recessive inheritance. When both parents are carriers, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of a child with the condition, a 50% chance of a carrier, and a 25% chance of neither altered copy in this model. Severity varies.Reviewed 12 March 2025; next review 12 March 2028. Present: Judge biological accuracy, traceable evidence and a clear limitation; not confidence, eye contact or amount of writing.3. Explain: For example: cystic fibrosis usually involves altered CFTR copies inherited from both parents. This affects salt/water movement and can lead to thick mucus affecting lungs and digestion.2. How these lessons are badged · 14 CONFORMS, 166 NOT YET

Current shows the lesson each week is actually taught from. A lesson is only moved to Earlier versions once a replacement for that same part of the week exists; until then it stays here, badged NOT YET, because it is the lesson being used. CONFORMS means the lesson’s own bytes carry the exemplar chassis (the PASS B census); the badge changes as lessons are rebuilt.
